slides.title: Star Spangled Banner
slides.body: Jimi Hendrix turns the final morning of Woodstock into a single, unmistakable guitar statement.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: The festival's scheduled closing set arrived Monday morning after delays. By then much of the crowd had gone, but the performance remained one of Woodstock's defining images.

slides.title: Soul Sacrifice
slides.body: A young Santana arrived at Woodstock with a sound that felt bigger than the band’s brief history.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: Santana played Saturday afternoon, only weeks after the release of its debut album. The set's Latin-rock fusion and Michael Shrieve's drum feature made the group a festival revelation.

slides.title: With A Little Help From My Friends
slides.body: Joe Cocker’s Woodstock breakthrough turned a Beatles song into a raw, soulful live signature.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: Cocker was still relatively unknown when he took the Sunday afternoon stage. His Grease Band arrangement became one of the performances most closely associated with Woodstock's public mythology.

slides.title: Freedom
slides.body: Ritchie Havens held the opening of Woodstock together when delays changed the festival’s first day.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: As the first performer, Havens was asked to continue while traffic kept other artists from the site. ‘Freedom’ grew from that pressure into an improvised finale based on ‘Motherless Child’.

slides.title: Work Me Lord
slides.body: Janis Joplin brought the full force of her voice to Woodstock’s Sunday night program.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: Joplin arrived at Woodstock already established as one of the era's most commanding singers. ‘Work Me Lord’ shows the performance not as a studio artifact, but as a high-wire exchange between voice, band, and exhausted festival crowd.

slides.title: Summertime Blues
slides.body: The Who’s Woodstock set carried the band’s hard-edged stage energy into the festival’s long night.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: The group arrived with Tommy behind it and a reputation for turning a stage into a physical event. ‘Summertime Blues’ is a compact view of that attack inside a festival built from scale and delay.

slides.title: Suite Judy Blue Eyes
slides.body: Crosby, Stills & Nash made their Woodstock debut as a new harmony unit under enormous attention.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: The trio was still early in its public life when it stepped onto the Woodstock stage. Their close vocal blend offered a different kind of spectacle: precision, harmony, and the feeling of a band becoming visible in real time.

slides.title: Going Up Country
slides.body: Canned Heat’s Woodstock appearance put a wandering, blues-rooted festival anthem in the middle of the weekend.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: ‘Going Up the Country’ had become one of Canned Heat's best-known songs by the time the band reached Bethel. Its country-bound refrain fit a festival where movement, escape, and temporary community were always in the air.

slides.title: If It Works
slides.body: Michael Lang speaks from inside the practical uncertainty of making Woodstock happen.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: The transcript captures an organizer answering questions while the festival is still an unfolding event. This is not a retrospective biography; it is a moment of production thinking under pressure, where success depends on adapting to conditions that cannot be fully controlled.

slides.title: Downpour
slides.body: Chip Monck’s announcement turns incoming rain into a shared instruction for hundreds of thousands of people.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: The existing transcript records the calm, practical language of the stage announcement: cover up, sit down, stay with one another, and wait out the weather. The scene shows Woodstock as logistics as much as legend.

slides.title: Max Yasgur's Benediction
slides.body: Max Yasgur addresses the crowd from the farm that became Woodstock’s temporary home.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: The recording is a public address from the landowner whose farm held the festival. Its value is direct and situational: the audience hears a host trying to speak to an enormous gathering at the point where event, community, and responsibility meet.

slides.title: Rain Chant
slides.body: Rain, mud, and collective endurance become the subject of this Woodstock crowd image.

slides.title: What you are watching
slides.body: This asset is visual context, not a quotation source. The stored transcript is ignored because crowd noise produced unreliable text. The useful evidence is the atmosphere: weather turning the festival into a shared physical experience.
